source.filename: 2010-Analytical and numerical analysis of multilayered beams with interlayer slip.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Plane sections remain plane for each constituent beam layer
Uniform transverse displacement across all layers without vertical separation or uplift (vi(x, y) = v(x))
Identical rotation for all constituent layers under Timoshenko beam kinematics
Linear elastic material behavior for all beam components (Hooke's law: Ni = (EA)i * dui/dx)
Linear elastic relationship for deformable interlayer connections (shear force Si = Ki * si)
Small displacements and small rotation kinematics
Negligible connection thickness modeled through zero-thickness interface kinematics
control_variables: Simply supported boundary conditions at member ends
Absence of applied axial end forces and zero curvature at ends
Zero transverse separation between adjacent layers along the beam span
Specified beam spans (300 cm for three-layer beam; 500 cm for four-layer beam)
dependent_variables: Interlayer slip distributions along the beam length (si(x))
Transverse displacements and maximum deflections (v(x), vmax)
Internal normal forces and bending moments along the layers

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The governing equations of multilayered beams with partial shear interaction can be expressed entirely in terms of interlayer slips, yielding a decoupled second-order ordinary differential equation system via eigenvalue transformation for statically determinate beams.
Interlayer slip distributions are identical under Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theories for statically determinate multilayered members.

The difference between Timoshenko and Euler-Bernoulli transverse deflections for a multilayered beam under uniform load depends solely on the aggregate shear stiffness (GA)0, matching the expression known for two-layered beams.

Combining conventional beam elements with zero-thickness interface elements accurately predicts interlayer slip and transverse deflections in multilayered composite members compared to closed-form solutions.

Using linear interpolation for axial displacements in interface elements causes severe slip and curvature locking under high connection stiffness, which is prevented by using at least quadratic axial interpolation.

independent_variables: Number of beam layers (3-layer and 4-layer configurations)
Interlayer connection shear stiffness (Ki, parameterized from flexible to near-rigid with gamma_i * L values of 1 and 50)
Elastic moduli and material properties of constituent layers (steel, concrete, and generic materials)
Cross-sectional geometry and dimensions of individual layers
Applied transverse loading conditions (uniformly distributed load q, central concentrated point load P)
Finite element mesh discretization density (4, 8, and 20 elements per interface)
Order of displacement interpolation polynomials (linear vs. quadratic axial interpolation)
limitations_inferred: Linear elastic and small-deflection assumptions prevent the modeling of large rotations, geometric non-linearities, or material yielding/damage at the connections.
Enforcing identical transverse deflection across all layers precludes consideration of cross-sectional deformation, through-thickness strain, or interlaminar separation under peeling forces.
The study does not model friction-based hysteretic sliding or active normal force modulation that would be relevant to controllable friction/jamming systems.
No experimental physical testing was conducted on physical specimens to validate the numerical or analytical predictions.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The slip-based analytical formulation requires the transverse shear force distribution V(x) to be known in advance, restricting closed-form solution derivation to statically determinate beams.
Transverse relative displacement (uplift) capabilities of the interface elements were not explored in the presented analyses.
Combining separate beam and interface elements increases the total number of system degrees of freedom compared to specialized multi-layer elements.
main_results: A new analytical formulation based exclusively on interlayer slip unknowns was established, reducing the coupled structural equations to a second-order ordinary differential equation system that uncouples through eigenvalue decomposition for statically determinate beams.
For statically determinate beams, the interlayer slip distribution is shown to be mathematically identical under both Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko kinematic assumptions.
The analytical discrepancy between Timoshenko and Euler-Bernoulli deflections for a uniformly loaded multilayered beam is exactly equal to q(Lx - x^2) / (2(GA)0).

In finite element simulations, Euler-Bernoulli models slightly underestimate exact slips whereas Timoshenko models overestimate them, with both converging to closed-form analytical results under mesh refinement.

Interface elements with linear axial displacement interpolation (ILC) suffer from curvature and slip locking when connection stiffness is high, whereas quadratic axial interpolation (IQC and ITQ) prevents locking.
modeling_methods: Euler-Bernoulli beam theory with partial interaction
Timoshenko beam theory with partial interaction and shear correction factors
Interlayer slip-based analytical formulation (system of second-order differential equations in slip variables)
Eigenvalue decoupling method for differential equations of statically determinate beams
Zero-thickness interface finite elements based on Goodman-Taylor-Brekke element kinematics
Interface Linear Cubic (ILC) finite element formulation
Interface Quadratic Cubic (IQC) finite element formulation
Interface Timoshenko Quadratic (ITQ) finite element formulation
performance_metrics: Numerical accuracy of interlayer slips and maximum transverse displacements relative to closed-form analytical solutions
Finite element convergence rate across mesh refinements (4, 8, 20 elements per interface)
Curvature and slip distribution fidelity under high connection stiffness (evaluation of slip/curvature locking)
possible_gap_implications: The interlayer slip formulation could provide a theoretical foundation for modeling layer-sliding and variable-stiffness laminar jamming structures in soft robotics, but requires extension to large deformations and controllable non-linear contact friction.
Analytical decoupling techniques for layered sliding may assist in formulating continuum manipulator compliance models if applied shear force distributions can be resolved along the backbone.
paper.research_objective: To investigate the mechanical behavior of generic multilayered composite beams with interlayer slip under Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theories, by developing an analytical formulation based solely on interlayer slip distributions and evaluating a numerical methodology coupling beam elements with zero-thickness interface elements to overcome slip and curvature locking.
paper.research_problem: The analytical and numerical complexity of modeling multilayered composite beams having multiple deformable interlayer slip planes, including coupled high-order governing differential equations and finite element slip/curvature locking under high connection stiffness.
stiffness_mechanism: deformable connections allowing relative horizontal slip between layers (partial interaction)
paper.title: Analytical and numerical analysis of multilayered beams with interlayer slip
